1:
Ellicott finds the placing of this chapter hard to account for. Holding the penalties for sins enumerated two chapters earlier, it should follow them at once; but it may be, he suggests, that before enacting punishments so severe the Lawgiver wished first to appeal to the nation's high calling by the precepts of the intervening chapter, so that what stands here is the civil alternative for those who will not be guided by them. Gill puts it more simply, that having delivered the laws God added penalties; and Wesley marks the same turn, that here follow the punishments of the crimes forbidden in the former chapters. Henry defends the repetition: it was no vain one, but necessary, that they might give the more earnest heed; God speaks once, yea twice, and what he orders said again we must be willing to hear again, because for us it is safe. He notes one change: in the earlier chapter the law about Molech follows the laws of incest, here it precedes them.

On the sacrifice Henry is unsparing. There is the grossest absurdity in all the rites of idolatry, he says, but none ever trampled so on the honours of human nature as this; it was plain evidence that their gods were devils, delighting in the misery and ruin of mankind, and that the worshippers were stripped not only of reason but of natural affection. He states the penalty as an exchange: if the children were sacrificed to the malice of the devil, the parents must be sacrificed to the justice of God. Calvin puts the offence in covenant terms, calling it a detestable sacrilege to enslave to idols an offspring begotten to God and adopted in the loins of Abraham, since by it men not only despoiled God of his right but blotted out the grace of adoption; and a general prohibition was not enough, since offenders would else have pleaded that they never meant to revolt to other gods. Henry finds the aggravation in what was peculiar to Israel: the Gentiles who sacrificed their children were guilty of murder and idolatry, but an Israelite incurred besides the guilt of defiling the sanctuary and profaning the name by which he was called. And where the magistrate would not act, misprision of idolatry remains cognizable in the court of heaven: if magistrates will not do justice on offenders, God will do justice on them.

Keil states the law plainly — whoever, Israelite or sojourner, gave of his children to Molech was to be stoned — and observes that in doing so the nation only carried out the will of Jehovah. Ellicott presses who the people of the land are: the whole community, in whose name sentence is passed, must execute it. Of the procedure laid down in the second Temple he notes that wine mingled with myrrh was given the condemned man to dull the pain, and that one witness pushed him from a scaffold while the other dashed a stone on his breast — which explains why Christ's accusers were told that he who was without sin should cast the first stone. Clarke reports the rabbinic descriptions of the idol — brass, man-shaped with an ox's head, a fire kindled inside and the child roasted in its arms — and then refuses them, questioning the whole truth of these statements, since there is no evidence of any of it in the sacred writings, and only presumptive proof, and that not strong, that human sacrifices were offered to Molech by the Jews at all. Passing through the fire, he thinks, may mean no more than a rite of consecration, perhaps an ordeal in which the person passed suddenly through the flame, or between two fires, scorched but neither killed nor consumed; and he sets beside it Caesar's account of the Druids, who burnt those adjudged to death inside an image of wickerwork.
3:
The declaration that God will cut the offender off has troubled them, since the verse before has the people stoning him already. Ellicott lays out two answers. Some take the words to express the same thing, judicial execution being God's own way of cutting a sinner off; but the second Temple authorities supposed a case where the man is genuinely guilty and there is not evidence enough to convict him, so that God himself interposes. Ellicott prefers the second, as more in accordance with what follows. On the charge of defiling the sanctuary Keil rejects one explanation: it is not, as Movers supposed, because the offender brought a sacrifice meant for Moloch into it, but in the same sense in which all Israel's sins defiled the sanctuary in their midst. Wesley adds that by such acts men declared they esteemed the sanctuary and service of God vile, preferring an odious idolatry before it, and profaned the name by giving others occasion to blaspheme it. Ellicott adds the detail that stings: these very people, having sacrificed their children, afterwards came to the sanctuary to worship.

The law then turns on the bystanders. Gill spells out who is meant by those who hide their eyes — the friends and neighbours who know what the man is about and look another way, or will not come forward and bear witness; or a court negligent in punishing, a gift having blinded its eyes. Keil takes the hiding of eyes to spring either from unscrupulous indifference or from secret approval of the sin, and notes that then the Lord would set his face against the man and his family and cut him off with all that went a whoring after him. Ellicott states the progression: the previous verse dealt with insufficient evidence, this one with what God will do if the community, whose duty it is to execute sentence, connives out of culpable indifference or criminal sympathy. Gill reads the threat as falling on the man who saw the act and winked at it, and on the judge who would not condemn, as well as on the doer. Keil observes that the same sentence covers those who turn to familiar spirits and wizards, such practices being always bound up with idolatry, and that the call to sanctify themselves means keeping clear of idolatrous abominations, being holy because Jehovah is holy. Wesley reads the ground of that call in the closing words: God separates them from all nations and their impurities to be a peculiar people, and gives them grace to keep his statutes.

With the cursing of parents the penalties proper begin, and Gill marks the order, that law having stood first in the earlier chapter. Keil notes that the crime was capital and that the formula about the man's blood means the guilt returns on the doer. Wesley narrows what is meant — not every perverse expression, but bitter reproaches or imprecations — and reads the formula as saying the man is guilty of his own death, deserving to die for so unnatural a crime. Clarke widens it the other way. The Hebrew verb signifies not only to curse but to speak of a person contemptuously, to make light of, so that all speeches tending to lessen our parents in the eyes of others may be included, though it is the act of cursing, the treating of a parent with opprobrious language, that is particularly intended. Ellicott records how far the later authorities narrowed the sentence in practice: they enacted that a child incurred death only if he used the ineffable name in cursing his parent, living or dead, and that if he used an attribute of the Deity instead, such as the Almighty or the Merciful, he was simply beaten with stripes — which is why the ancient Chaldee renders the clause of one who curses by the inexpressible name.
10:
Henry explains why the penalties are set so high. These are sins which of all others fools are most apt to make a mock at, and God would teach the heinousness of the guilt by the extremity of the punishment to those who would not otherwise learn it. Adultery he calls a presumptuous contempt of an ordinance of God, an irreparable wrong to the injured husband, and a sin which headstrong and unbridled lusts hurry men violently into, so that it needs a restraint of just this force; it defiles a land and brings down God's judgments on it, and tends to the ruin of all virtue and religion. Yet Henry sets one reference against the whole paragraph, pointing the reader to the woman brought to Christ. Clarke pauses on the word itself, which comes from the Latin, compounded of the preposition meaning to and the word for another, or, as some derive it, from a phrase for one who approaches another man's bed. Ellicott gives the Jewish rule of construction: wherever the formula that a man shall surely be put to death stands by itself, without a mode named, tradition takes it of strangling, a death inflicted for six crimes, of which adultery is the first.

Calvin explains what this chapter does that the earlier one did not. Nothing new occurs here, he says, the object being by penalties to sanction the instruction lately given: by condemning incestuous marriages before, Moses cited the Israelites before God, so that conscience might abhor the crime although they had nothing to fear from earthly judges; now he alarms them with the dread of punishment. He does not chastise the incestuous with rods, as if theirs were a light offence, but pronounces it a capital crime where a man has sinned against the law of nature. On the case of a woman and her mother Calvin enters a careful qualification: the punishment reaches the mother also, but only if she consents, for if a man seduces the daughter against her mother's will, and the mother cannot resist it though she would, she is free from guilt.

The formula that their blood shall be upon them is read as a charge to the judges. Calvin takes it to mean that the cause of their death is to be imputed to none but the criminals themselves, and thinks it set down lest judges, under the cloak of humanity, should shrink from severity — since those who do not sufficiently weigh the atrocity of an evil are often led away by an empty show of clemency. Moses hints indirectly, he adds, that if the guilty are pardoned vengeance will be provoked against the whole people, iniquity being fostered by impunity until it bursts out like a deluge. Where the sentence is childlessness rather than death, Calvin finds the penalty answering to the crime, since it is just that those be exterminated in barrenness who had endeavoured to corrupt the holy race of Abraham with an adulterous seed. Henry reads that milder sentence the same way: those who keep not within the divine rules of marriage forfeit the blessings of marriage, and though such offenders are not immediately cut off by the hand of God or man, the guilt shall lie upon them, to be reckoned for at another day, and shall not be purged with sacrifice. Gill shows how little the wording leaves open on the father's wife, since it matters not whether she was his own mother or a stepmother, in his father's lifetime or after, betrothed or married; and Wesley explains the word rendered confusion as perverting the order God appointed, and making the same offspring both a man's own child and his grandchild. Keil ranks the penalties as the text gives them, noting that where a man took a wife and her mother the punishment was heightened by burning after death.
15:
Wesley explains why the beast was to be killed along with the offender: partly for the prevention of monstrous births, and partly to blot out the memory of so loathsome a crime. Clarke supplies the historical setting, and thinks it explains more than this one law. He cites Herodotus as an eyewitness that such a thing happened openly in one Egyptian district within his own recollection, and draws the conclusion: need we wonder that God made laws of this nature, when it appears these abominations were not only practised among the Egyptians but formed parts of a superstitious religious system? That one observation, Clarke says, will account for many of the strange prohibitions in the Mosaic law; and as for the others, whose reasons are not so plain, we should see their propriety equally well had we fuller records of the customs of that country.

On the sister Wesley returns to the question he had raised in the earlier chapter, and finds this passage settles it: in this and several of the following verses, he says, uncovering nakedness plainly appears to mean not marriage but fornication or adultery. Gill draws a distinction the penalty requires at the next law, since a man who lay with his wife in ignorance was unclean seven days only, whereas the cutting off falls where both knew what they did. Calvin reasons from the severity back to the offence. The enormity of the crime is seen in the punishment, he says, for when a man and woman abandon themselves to so disgraceful an act it is plain there are no remains of modesty left in them; God regards not only the offence itself but the brutal impulse of lust by which men are carried away until they degenerate from the very feelings of nature. What wickedness would he abstain from, Calvin asks, who yields to such impurity that in his fury he breaks through an obstacle which restrains the brutes themselves? He allows that a woman in that state is withheld from a man by the foulness of the case and the danger of contagion, but insists that God chooses here to be an instructor in decency to his people rather than to perform the office of a physician; the precept has no other tendency than that believers should be kept far from all filthiness and that chastity may flourish among them, and married persons in particular are exhorted to restrain themselves from all immodest lasciviousness, the husband enjoying his wife's company with delicacy and propriety.

Where the sentence changes from death to childlessness the commentators pause over what it means. Wesley offers two readings, either that the offenders shall be speedily cut off before they can have a child by that conjunction, or — if the crime seem a lesser one than most of those before it, so that the magistrate forbears to punish it with death — that they shall either have no children at all from such an unlawful bed, or their children shall die before them. Ellicott refers each of these cases back, one by one, to the prohibition it answers in the earlier chapter. Gill notes the one standing exception on the brother's wife, that where there was no issue a man was obliged by another law to take her, though that law has since ceased, so that the prohibition now stands clear of exceptions; and Wesley says the same in a line, excepting only the case God himself allowed. Keil looks ahead to how the list is rounded off, observing that the catalogue of punishments closes, as the catalogue of prohibitions did, with exhortations to keep the commandments of the Lord and avoid such abominations, the reason assigned being that Jehovah was about to give them the fruitful land whose inhabitants he had driven out for these very things.
22:
Ellicott notes that the penalties close as the prohibitions did, with an appeal to keep the divine precepts and not repeat the crimes for which the former inhabitants were cast out; and he would render the warning lest the land vomit you out. Clarke draws the historical conclusion from that figure: the cup of the iniquities of the Canaanites was full, so that consistently with divine justice they could be spared no longer. Gill observes that the nation named stands for the seven, though some take it of the Amorites, whose wickedness made their way a byword. Keil adds that because Israel was called to be the holy nation of Jehovah, the same separation reached even to the beasts they might eat. Calvin marks this as the third warning against imitating the Gentiles, and notes that Israel inherited the land only on terms of separating from the heathen.

Henry gathers the closing verses under three heads. First their dignity: they had the Lord for their God, being his care, his choice, his treasure, his jewels; his holiness is his glory, so that it was their honour to be related to him while their neighbours worshipped impure spirits; and he had separated them, so that where other nations were the common, they were the enclosure. Second their duty, since God had done more for them and expected more: to keep all his statutes; not to walk in the manners of the nations, since being separated they must not learn their ways; and to put a difference between clean and unclean — for this, Henry says, is holiness, to discern between things that differ, not to live at large as if we might say and do anything, but to speak and act with caution. Third their danger: they were going into an infected place, a land flowing with milk and honey but full of idols they would be apt to fall in love with. See what an evil thing sin is, Henry says, that it provokes God to abhor his own creatures, whereas otherwise he delights in the work of his hands. And if God spared not the natural branches, neither would he spare those grafted in; the rejection of the Jews stands as a warning to all Christian churches lest the kingdom of God be taken from them.

On clean and unclean Ellicott presses a matter of translation. The verb is the one rendered separate at the close of the previous verse, and it matters that English keep the same word, since this shows the connection and brings out the reason: because the Lord has separated the Israelites and is about to give them the land, they are to separate the clean animal from the unclean, and so keep themselves apart. Calvin reaches the same conclusion from the other end, so that the animals were forbidden for no other reason than that the people might learn to withdraw far from all the pollutions of the Gentiles; there would be something unmeaning in the words, he says, if we did not know the interdiction was imposed with that object. Ellicott closes with the generous reading the later authorities gave that doctrine of separation, that it implies no rejection of the other nations but is only a first instalment. Had Scripture said, I have separated all the nations from you, there would be no future for the Gentiles; but since it says, I have separated you from the nations, it is as one who first sets apart the best from the less good and goes on separating the better, whereas he who separates the bad from the good by that act rejects the bad and does not return. So understood, the doctrine, far from breeding contracted views of God's mercy, taught the Jews to look on themselves as having simply gone first to the mountain of the Lord, all other nations to follow.
27:
Ellicott begins with the conjunction, which he thinks should not have been softened in the Authorised Version and is better given as but: because the Israelites are God's holy ones, therefore every man or woman who pretends to disclose future events by necromancy, and so usurps the functions of God, is to be stoned to death. He explains why the case appears a third time. In the earlier chapter only the consulting of such people was forbidden; at the sixth verse of this chapter the penalty for consulting them was set down; and here at last the penalty is enacted against the practitioners themselves, who are convicted of the secret arts. Ellicott gives two reasons why the woman is expressly named, both because the art seems to have been principally followed by women, and because men would naturally be inclined to treat women more mercifully; and he takes the closing formula, as at the earlier verse, to mean that they have brought their death upon themselves.

Gill arrives at the same two reasons from the rabbis. Aben Ezra observed that such practices were more frequently committed by women, and Maimonides added that men have a natural clemency toward the female sex and are not easily prevailed upon to put them to death — which is why the law elsewhere says expressly that a witch shall not be suffered to live. Gill defines the second offender as a knowing one, who pretends to great knowledge of things, of goods lost or stolen and even of things to come, and so imposes upon people and cheats them of the money they give for the information; and he presses that such were not to be spared through favour or affection. Clarke defines the first as a spirit or demon which, by magical rites, is supposed to be bound to appear at the call of the man who employs it. Wesley states the sentence in a phrase that carries its own reason: those who are in league with the devil have in effect made a covenant with death, and so shall their doom be.

Clarke closes the chapter by standing back from it. From the accounts we have of the abominations of both Egypt and Canaan, he says, we may blush for human nature; for wherever human nature is without cultivation and without the revelation of God, it is everything vile in principle and detestable in practice. Nor would any part of the habitable globe differ materially from Egypt and Canaan, he adds, had they not that rule of righteousness, the revealed law of God, and had not life and immortality been brought to light by the gospel among them. From such accounts, for which he grants that parallels could easily be found in ancient Greece and Italy, Clarke draws the conclusion the whole chapter has been building toward: that we may see from them the absolute need of a divine revelation, without which man, even in his best estate, differs little from the brute.
